title: The Amistad: Voices Through an Interpreter
subtitle: The Amistad revolt, the Connecticut courts and the Supreme Court, 1839–1842
intro: Before dawn on 2 July 1839, off the north coast of Cuba, fifty-three Africans held on the Spanish schooner Amistad broke free and took the ship. The captain and the cook were killed and two sailors escaped in a boat. Two Cuban buyers, José Ruiz and Pedro Montes, were spared to sail the ship east to Africa. For eight weeks Montes steered east by day and north-west by night. On 26 August 1839 a US Navy survey brig, the Washington, found the schooner anchored off Culloden Point at the eastern end of Long Island and took it into New London, Connecticut.

What followed was not one trial but a chain of them. There was a hearing on the deck of a warship, a grand jury and habeas corpus hearing in Hartford, and suits for false imprisonment in New York. A district-court trial in New Haven in January 1840 was followed by a pro forma appeal and then eight days of argument before the Supreme Court in Washington in February and March 1841. On every side were claims of property: the naval officers claimed salvage, the Cuban buyers wanted their 'slaves' back, and the Spanish government invoked a treaty. The Van Buren administration kept a navy schooner waiting in New Haven harbour in case the verdict went against the Africans.

The chapter gives priority to the captives' own voices. Almost everything they said reached the record through an interpreter. For the first five weeks there was none who spoke Mende, until the Yale philologist Josiah Gibbs found James Covey, a young sailor on a British warship who had himself been freed from a slave ship. Sengbe Pieh (called Cinqué by the Americans), Grabeau and Fuliwa told their story through Covey in depositions and in court, and newspapers and Barber's 1840 pamphlet printed it in shortened and edited English. By January 1841 Kale and Kinna, two of the younger men, were writing letters in their own new English to John Quincy Adams. Each entry says whether the words passed through someone else.

Few of these sources are diaries. The exceptions are John Quincy Adams's daily journal and, more briefly, Lewis Tappan's. The rest are court records (libels, decrees and the Supreme Court's opinion), an executive order, diplomatic notes, newspaper reports and dated letters, and the form tags say so. Some famous lines have doubtful origins. The most quoted words attributed to Cinqué, printed in New York before any interpreter had been found, are one example. The story told a century later, that he became a slave trader after going home, is another. Historians have traced it to a 1946 book and found no evidence for it.

The courts did not decide whether the revolt was justified as a moral question. The Supreme Court held on 9 March 1841 that the Africans had been kidnapped and illegally imported into Cuba and were not property under Spanish law, so they were free. It also overturned the lower court's order handing them to the President for removal, so they were simply released. No public money paid for their passage home. Thirty-five survivors sailed from New York in late November 1841 with missionaries and reached Sierra Leone in January 1842.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian and need no conversion. Some dates differ between sources. Judge Judson announced his decision on 13 January 1840, but the recorded decree is dated 23 January. The sailing from New York is given as 27 November 1841 by the National Park Service, while one account dates Tappan's farewell on board to 4 December. A letter signed by Cinqué is dated '29 February 1841', a day that did not exist in 1841. Dates are shown as the documents give them, with ranges where the record is uncertain.

eyes.name: Sengbe Pieh (called Cinqué or Cinquez)
eyes.role: Mende rice farmer from Mani, about 25 in 1839, married with three children; leader of the revolt and principal witness
eyes.where: Aboard the Amistad; New Haven jail and Westville; Farmington; home to Sierra Leone
eyes.vantage_label: leader of the revolt, speaking through an interpreter
eyes.form: testimony through interpreters (as reported); dictated or assisted letters
eyes.authenticity: Cinqué left no writing in Mende. His words survive as English renderings. Before October 1839 only a few phrases were passed on through Antonio, the cabin boy, and Bernar, one of the captives, who spoke a little English. After that his words came through James Covey, in depositions, in court testimony reported by the New York Journal of Commerce (10 January 1840), and in John Warner Barber's edited sketches (New Haven, 1840). Letters signed by him in February 1841 (Baldwin Family Papers, Yale; another to Lewis Tappan) were written in English with help. The speech printed under his name by the New York Sun in August 1839 has no stated source. The later story that he became a slave trader is traced by historians to a 1946 book and is unsupported.
eyes.bio: Sengbe was seized on a road in the Mende country, sold at the Lomboko slave factory, carried to Havana on the Portuguese ship Tecora and bought by José Ruiz. He freed himself and the others from their irons on the Amistad and led the revolt. In court in New Haven he told the story of his capture through Covey. He returned to Sierra Leone in 1842, and missionary records place him at the Mende mission again near the end of his life.

eyes.name: Grabeau (Gilabaru)
eyes.role: Mende captive, second in authority after Sengbe; witness in court
eyes.where: New Haven jail; district court, New Haven
eyes.vantage_label: a leader among the captives, narrator of the Middle Passage
eyes.form: narrative and testimony through an interpreter (as reported)
eyes.authenticity: His account of the voyage from Africa to Havana, given through Covey on 7 October 1839, was printed in the New York Journal of Commerce and in Barber's pamphlet (1840). It is a reporter's English summary and not a transcript. He testified again at the January 1840 trial.
eyes.bio: Grabeau was the first captive to recognise the Mende numbers that Josiah Gibbs counted out in the jail, and was among the first to give a full narrative once Covey arrived. His account of the Tecora's hold, confirmed by the others, became the defence's evidence that the men were newly brought from Africa and not long-time Cuban slaves.

sources.title: Barber, History of the Amistad Captives (1840)
Famous Trials: newspaper accounts (Journal of Commerce narrative)

eyes.name: Kale
eyes.role: Young Mende captive taught English in the New Haven and Westville jails; writer of the letter to Adams
eyes.vantage_label: a captive writing in his own new English
eyes.language: English (learned in captivity); native language Mende
eyes.authenticity: The original letter of 4 January 1841 is in the Adams Family Papers, Massachusetts Historical Society. A transcription was printed by Simon E. Baldwin in Papers of the New Haven Colony Historical Society vol. 4 (1888). Kinna's letter of the same month survives with it. Kale's English was learned from Yale students and local teachers, who may have helped. The letter is his own composition in style, but some help cannot be ruled out.
eyes.bio: Barber's 1840 sketch describes Kale as young and pleasant, seized on his way to buy rice. Over sixteen months of lessons he learned to read and write English. Seven weeks before Adams was to speak, he wrote to him on behalf of all the captives. It is the fullest statement in their own words that survives.

sources.title: MHS Object of the Month, January 2003: Kale's and Kinna's letters
Kale to JQA, 4 Jan 1841 (transcription, TeachIt CT)

eyes.name: James Benjamin Covey (Kaweli)
eyes.role: Mende-born sailor on the British brig-of-war Buzzard, himself freed from a slave ship; court interpreter
eyes.side: Sierra Leone liberated African; Royal Navy
eyes.where: HMS Buzzard at New York; New Haven jail and courts

waypoints.label: HMS Buzzard, New York harbour, Oct 1839

eyes.vantage_label: the interpreter through whom the captives spoke
eyes.authenticity: His deposition dated 4 October 1839 is in the Baldwin Family Papers, Yale. His work in court is recorded in the district-court papers and newspaper reports. His age is uncertain: some accounts make him about fourteen, others about twenty. He sailed home with the captives on the Gentleman.
eyes.bio: Kidnapped as a child and carried to Lomboko, Covey was freed when a British cruiser took the slave ship carrying him. He was educated by missionaries in Sierra Leone and joined the Royal Navy. Gibbs found him on the Buzzard in New York, and for over a year almost every word the captives said in court passed through him.

sources.title: Connecticut History: the teenager who helped save the Mende captives
Yale News: the Amistad affair in Yale Library's collections (Covey deposition, 4 Oct 1839)

eyes.name: Josiah Willard Gibbs Sr.
eyes.role: Professor of sacred literature and philologist at Yale, aged 49
eyes.where: New Haven jail; New York waterfront; witness stand
eyes.vantage_label: the linguist who gave the captives a voice
eyes.form: vocabulary notes, published word list and court testimony
eyes.authenticity: His Mende word list was published in the American Journal of Science (1840). His trial testimony is in the district-court record and newspaper reports. The story of his counting in Mende along the docks comes from his own and Barber's accounts. The exact day he found Covey is not recorded, and NPS and Barber disagree on it.
eyes.bio: Gibbs learned the Mende numbers one to ten from the captives by holding up fingers and coins, then walked the waterfront counting aloud until a sailor answered. In court he argued that the captives' names were Mende words, unchanged by any years in Cuba. He was the father of the physicist J. Willard Gibbs.

sources.title: Famous Trials: biography of Josiah Gibbs
NPS detailed Amistad timeline

eyes.name: Lewis Tappan
eyes.role: New York silk merchant and evangelical abolitionist, aged 51; leading member of the Amistad Committee
eyes.where: New York; frequent visits to New Haven and Farmington

waypoints.label: New York, suits against Ruiz and Montes, Oct 1839

eyes.vantage_label: organiser of the defence, writing to the press
eyes.form: letters to the press, private letters and journal
eyes.authenticity: Tappan's letters were printed in the New York Journal of Commerce and the Emancipator in 1839–41. His letters to the British abolitionists Joseph Sturge and John Scoble and his journal are among his papers at the Library of Congress. The Amistad Committee's dated appeals and reports were published as pamphlets. He was a committed partisan, and his descriptions of the captives were meant to win public sympathy.
eyes.bio: Tappan raised money, hired counsel, organised the captives' teaching and kept the case in the press for two and a half years. His suits against Ruiz and Montes in New York turned the claimants into defendants. He recruited John Quincy Adams for the Supreme Court and organised the return voyage and the Mende mission, which grew into the American Missionary Association.

sources.title: D. Linder, 'Stamped with Glory: Lewis Tappan and the Africans of the Amistad' (Famous Trials)
JOC history: 'The captives are freed'
NPS: the Amistad Committee

eyes.name: Roger Sherman Baldwin
eyes.role: New Haven lawyer, aged 46; chief counsel ('proctor') for the Africans in every court
eyes.where: Hartford and New Haven courts; Supreme Court, Washington
eyes.form: court pleadings, printed argument and letters
eyes.authenticity: His pleas, answers and notes survive in the district-court records (National Archives) and the Baldwin Family Papers (Yale). His Supreme Court argument was printed in 1841 and is in Peters' Reports. These are an advocate's documents, written to persuade.
eyes.bio: Baldwin was among the first to interview Cinqué and stayed with the case from the deck of the Washington to the Supreme Court. His central argument was that men brought from Africa to Cuba after Spain's 1817 treaty with Britain could not lawfully be slaves under Spanish law. The Supreme Court adopted that reasoning. He was a grandson of Roger Sherman.

sources.title: Federal Judicial Center: The Amistad Trials (case history and documents)
National Archives at Boston: Amistad featured document

eyes.name: John Quincy Adams
eyes.role: Former President, aged 72–74; congressman from Massachusetts; counsel for the Africans before the Supreme Court
eyes.where: Washington (House of Representatives and Supreme Court); Quincy, Massachusetts; visit to New Haven
eyes.vantage_label: the old statesman who argued in court
eyes.authenticity: Adams kept a daily diary for nearly seventy years. It is in the Adams Family Papers at the Massachusetts Historical Society, which has digitised it, and extracts were printed in the Memoirs of John Quincy Adams (1874–77). His argument was published by S. W. Benedict, New York, in 1841 from his own revised text. It is longer and more polished than what he said in court. Peters' Reports left it out.
eyes.bio: Adams had followed the case in his diary from October 1839 and agreed to argue it only in October 1840, citing his age. He visited the captives in their jail before the hearing. In the Supreme Court he spoke for about eight hours over two days, attacking the executive's conduct as much as the Spanish claim. His diary records how he worried over it beforehand, his relief at the verdict, and his later attempts to get the Africans home.

sources.title: JQA Digital Diary, 27 Oct 1840 (MHS)
MHS: Amistad selected topic (diary entries list)
MHS Beehive: 'My conscience presses me on'
Argument of John Quincy Adams (1841), Avalon Project

eyes.name: Lieutenant Thomas R. Gedney, USN (and the brig Washington)
eyes.role: Commander of the US Coast Survey brig Washington, aged about 40; salvage claimant
eyes.where: Off Culloden Point, Long Island; New London harbour
eyes.vantage_label: the officer who seized the ship and claimed salvage
eyes.form: official account and libel for salvage (court record)
eyes.authenticity: The account of the capture dated New London, 26 August 1839, was printed in the press and reprinted by Barber (1840). Gedney's libel of 29 August 1839, filed with Lieutenant Richard W. Meade, who led the boarding party, is in the district-court records (National Archives, RG 21). It is a legal claim, and its figures are valuations meant to win salvage.
eyes.bio: Gedney's brig was surveying the coast when its officers saw the schooner and men on the shore. He brought the ship into Connecticut rather than New York, which defence counsel later suggested was because Connecticut still allowed slavery in law. He claimed salvage on the vessel, the cargo and the Africans as property.

sources.title: Prologue (NARA): The Amistad case in the National Archives, part 2
Barber (1840), official account of the capture

eyes.name: José Ruiz and Pedro Montes, and the Spanish legation (Ángel Calderón de la Barca)
eyes.life: Ruiz and Montes fl. 1839; Calderón de la Barca 1790–1861
eyes.role: Ruiz, a young Cuban planter's agent, bought 49 men; Montes, an older merchant and former ship captain, bought four children. Calderón de la Barca was Spain's minister in Washington.
eyes.where: Aboard the Amistad; New London; New York; Washington
eyes.vantage_label: the men who claimed the captives as property
eyes.form: sworn statements and libels (court record); published letter; diplomatic notes
eyes.authenticity: Their statements at New London were taken through a translator and summarised in the court record and the press. Their libels of 18 September 1839 are in the district-court records. Their published letter of thanks to Gedney appeared in Connecticut newspapers. The Spanish minister's notes to Secretary of State Forsyth were printed by Congress in 1840–41 among the Amistad correspondence. These are partisan documents, and the passports they relied on described the captives falsely as 'ladinos', long-resident slaves.
eyes.bio: Ruiz and Montes had been forced at knifepoint to sail the Amistad for eight weeks. They reached New London as rescued men and soon became defendants in New York suits. Spain's minister argued that under the 1795 treaty the ship and its 'merchandise' must be returned, and that the Africans should be tried in Cuba. The claim was renewed for years after 1841.

sources.title: NPS detailed Amistad timeline
Office of the Historian: The Amistad case
Famous Trials: newspaper accounts (Ruiz and Montes letter)

eyes.name: Andrew T. Judson
eyes.role: US District Judge for Connecticut, aged 55; a Democrat who had prosecuted Prudence Crandall's school for Black girls in 1833
eyes.side: Federal district court (record of the court)
eyes.where: Aboard the Washington at New London; Hartford; New Haven
eyes.authenticity: The district-court files, including the warrants, libels, answers and the decree recorded on 23 January 1840, are in the National Archives (RG 21). His spoken decision of 13 January 1840 was reported in the press and printed by Barber. He was widely expected to rule for the government. He ruled the other way.
eyes.bio: Judson held the first hearing on a warship's deck four days after the seizure. Sixteen months later he found that the Africans were born free and had been kidnapped. Their passports were false, he held, and they should be delivered to the President for return to Africa. He awarded salvage on the ship and cargo but not on the people.

sources.title: Federal Judicial Center: The Amistad Trials
Famous Trials: trial testimony and decree

eyes.name: President Martin Van Buren and Secretary of State John Forsyth
eyes.role: President (aged 56, seeking re-election in 1840) and his Secretary of State, a Georgian
eyes.vantage_label: the government that wanted the captives sent to Cuba
eyes.form: executive orders, instructions and diplomatic correspondence
eyes.authenticity: The order of 7 January 1840 signed by Van Buren and countersigned by Forsyth survives (Gilder Lehrman Collection, GLC05636.01). Forsyth's instructions to the district attorney and his notes to the Spanish minister were printed in the House documents of 1840–41. Adams later charged that a translation in these documents had been altered, and in December 1840 a House committee was set up to examine it.
eyes.bio: The administration accepted Spain's view that the ship and Africans should be returned under the 1795 treaty and did not want a public trial in a free state. It had the navy schooner Grampus ready at New Haven to take the Africans out of the country at once if Judson ruled against them, before any appeal. When he ruled for them, it appealed.

sources.title: Van Buren order for transport of the Amistad captives, 7 Jan 1840 (Gilder Lehrman / AM Digital)
Office of the Historian: The Amistad case

eyes.name: Joseph Story
eyes.role: Associate Justice of the US Supreme Court, aged 61; also Dane Professor of Law at Harvard
eyes.where: Supreme Court chamber, US Capitol, Washington; home at Cambridge, Massachusetts
eyes.vantage_label: the justice who wrote the opinion
eyes.form: court opinion (US Reports) and dated letters
eyes.authenticity: The opinion of 9 March 1841 is printed as United States v. The Amistad, 40 U.S. (15 Peters) 518. Story's letters to his wife were published by his son William Wetmore Story in Life and Letters of Joseph Story (1851). The letter describing Adams's argument is cited in that edition, but its exact date was not checked here.
eyes.bio: Story had sat on the Court since 1811 and had condemned the slave trade from the bench in 1820s circuit cases. Writing for the majority, with one justice dissenting, he held the Spanish documents fraudulent and the Africans kidnapped. He also held they could lawfully resist and could not be handed to the executive. Privately he found Adams's speech powerful but far outside the record.

sources.title: NARA DocsTeach: Opinion of the Supreme Court in United States v. the Amistad
Library of Congress, Today in History: 9 March

eyes.name: Connecticut and New York newspapers (New London Gazette, New York Sun, Journal of Commerce, Hartford Courant)
eyes.role: Reporters, editors and letter-writers who carried the case to the public, and through it the crowd outside
eyes.where: New London, New York, Hartford, New Haven

waypoints.label: New York Sun and Journal of Commerce

eyes.authenticity: Reports survive in the original papers and in compilations, including Barber (1840) and Douglas Linder's Famous Trials texts. Many were reprinted from one paper to another with changes. The New York Sun sold a lithograph of 'Cinquez' with a speech whose source was never given. The Journal of Commerce was close to Tappan and the Hartford Courant was a Whig paper opposed to Van Buren.
eyes.bio: The press shaped the case from the first rumour of a 'long, low, black schooner' off Long Island. Papers sold prints of Cinqué, reported the crowds at the jail and the trial, printed the captives' stories through Covey, and turned the Grampus into a scandal in an election year.

sources.title: Famous Trials: newspaper accounts of the Amistad
LOC: 'Joseph Cinquez, the brave Congolese Chief' (lithograph, 1839)

entries.headline: Ruiz and Montes sail with their purchases
entries.digest: José Ruiz had bought forty-nine adult men in Havana and Pedro Montes four children, three girls and a boy. They took them aboard the coastal schooner Amistad, Captain Ramón Ferrer, bound for Puerto Príncipe. Passports issued between 22 and 26 June described the Africans as 'ladinos', slaves long resident in Cuba. All of them had been brought from Africa that spring, in breach of Spain's 1817 treaty with Britain.
entries.source_note: NPS detailed timeline (28 June boarding; passports 22–26 June); FJC case history (Tecora from Lomboko; passes describing them as residents).

entries.date_display: Tuesday 2 July 1839, about 4 a.m. (as later told through Covey)
entries.place: Aboard the Amistad, off the north coast of Cuba
entries.headline: The irons come off; the ship is taken
entries.digest: By his own later account, Sengbe worked loose his collar and freed himself and Grabeau the night before, then the others. Before dawn they found cane knives in the hold and rose. Captain Ferrer and the cook were killed and two crewmen got away in a boat. Ruiz and Montes were wounded, then spared to sail the ship back toward the sunrise and Africa. In court he said the cook had told them by signs that they would be killed and eaten. That threat is what decided them.
entries.source_note: NPS timeline (1 July freeing; 2 July c. 4 a.m. revolt); Cinqué's testimony through Covey, NY Journal of Commerce 10 Jan 1840; Connecticut History (cook's threat as told through Covey). The account is his, rendered in English by others.

entries.place: Aboard the Amistad, Caribbean and Atlantic
entries.headline: East by day, north-west by night
entries.digest: Kept at work under guard, Montes, who had been a sea captain, steered toward the rising sun in daylight as ordered. By night he turned north and west, hoping to meet a warship or reach the American coast. Food and water ran short and several Africans died on the voyage. Their own account says they had no idea where the ship was going.
entries.source_note: FJC case history; Ruiz and Montes statements at New London (summarised in press). Day range approximate.

entries.place: Off Culloden Point, Montauk, Long Island
entries.headline: The Washington's boat boards a strange schooner
entries.digest: Officers of the survey brig Washington saw a battered schooner at anchor and men ashore buying supplies with Spanish doubloons. Lieutenant Meade's boat party boarded. Ruiz and Montes came forward as rescued owners, and the Africans ashore and on deck were secured, Cinqué after trying to escape by jumping overboard. An account of the capture dated New London that day went to the papers and was reprinted by Barber the next year.
entries.source_note: Barber (1840), official account dated New London 26 Aug 1839; NPS timeline; Prologue (NARA) 2003, part 2.

entries.headline: The 'long, low, black schooner' is brought in
entries.digest: The New London Gazette told readers that a pilot-boat rumour had become a prize ship. In its account, the Africans had killed the captain and part of the crew and were trying to get back to Africa. A later dispatch described visiting the Washington and the leader in irons. It used the stock insults of the day for him, alongside wonder at his strength. For days the papers had printed sightings of a mysterious pirate off Long Island.
entries.quote: intention of returning to the coast of Africa
entries.source_note: New London Gazette, 26 Aug 1839 and 'Tuesday, 12 o'clock' dispatch, as given in Famous Trials newspaper accounts; Barber introduction for the 'long, low, black schooner' phrase.

entries.place: Aboard the brig Washington, New London harbour
entries.headline: A court on a warship's deck
entries.digest: Judge Judson held a special session of the district court on board the Washington, then moved to the Amistad itself. There Antonio, the captain's enslaved cabin boy, pointed out the leaders of the revolt. Judson heard Ruiz and Montes and the salvage claim. He referred the charges of murder and piracy to the circuit court's grand jury and issued warrants to arrest the men and seize the 'property'. The Africans were sent to the county jail in New Haven.
entries.source_note: FJC case history; Barber (1840), court session 29 Aug; Prologue (NARA).

entries.headline: A libel for salvage: ship, cargo and people
entries.digest: Gedney and Lieutenant Meade filed a libel claiming salvage for rescuing the vessel. They valued the ship and cargo at about $40,000 and the Africans, as slaves, at $25,000. The claim treated the captives as property to be shared out by the court.
entries.source_note: Prologue (NARA) 2003, n. 4 (libel dated 29 Aug 1839); FJC case history (valuations); district-court records RG 21.

entries.date_display: 29 August 1839 (statements); letter of thanks published soon after
entries.headline: Rescued owners thank the Navy
entries.digest: Ruiz and Montes described the purchase in Havana and the night of the revolt, presenting themselves as victims of mutiny and murder. In a letter printed in the local papers they thanked Gedney and his crew for saving their lives and protecting their property, and praised the Spanish nation and its queen. They expected to take their slaves home.
entries.quote: their most unhoped for and most providential rescue
entries.source_note: FJC case history (statements at the hearing); Famous Trials newspaper accounts (letter of thanks, issue date not stated).

entries.headline: The Sun sells a hero's portrait, with a speech
entries.digest: The New York Sun advertised a lithograph of 'Joseph Cinquez, the brave Congolese Chief, who prefers death to slavery'. Its text included a speech he was said to have made to his comrades. The speech was printed before anyone who spoke Mende had talked with the captives, and its source is not stated. The famous words owe more to the Sun than to any record.
entries.quote: it is better to die than to be a white man's slave
entries.source_note: LOC item 2003690782 (print commissioned by the Sun, advertised 31 Aug 1839; quoted text as catalogued). Quote shortened from the longer catalogued passage. FLAG: attribution to Cinqué unverified.

entries.headline: A committee for the 'Friends of the Africans'
entries.digest: Tappan, the Reverend Joshua Leavitt and the Reverend Simeon Jocelyn formed a committee to hire counsel, raise funds and look after the captives. Their dated appeal asked the public for money for men who knew no English and had no friends in the country. They engaged Roger Baldwin, Seth Staples and Theodore Sedgwick.
entries.source_note: NPS timeline (4 Sept); Linder, 'Stamped with Glory' (appeal dated New York 4 Sept).

entries.headline: Spain demands the ship and its 'cargo'
entries.digest: Spain's minister, Ángel Calderón de la Barca, wrote to Secretary of State Forsyth demanding that the Amistad and everything aboard be handed back under the 1795 treaty. He asked that the Africans be sent to Cuba for trial by Spanish courts and that no salvage be paid. His note treated the matter as an executive question that American judges should not decide.
entries.source_note: NPS timeline (6 Sept demand); Office of the Historian (demand under the 1795 treaty). Note printed in the House documents on the Amistad correspondence.

entries.headline: First visit: a crowded jail and a tall leader
entries.digest: Tappan made his first visit to the jail and sent the Journal of Commerce a description of the men, the four children and the crowds paying to look at them. He described Cinqué as about five feet eight inches tall, finely proportioned and with a noble bearing. With no interpreter, he could only distribute tracts, attend prayers and watch.
entries.quote: of fine proportions, with a noble air
entries.source_note: Linder, 'Stamped with Glory' (first visit 6 Sept 1839); JOC history page (article dated 6 Sept 1839). Day of publication versus day of writing not distinguished.

entries.headline: Four claims on the same people
entries.digest: Judson opened the district-court session on the libels. Gedney claimed salvage, Ruiz and Montes their property, and the Long Island men who had met the shore party a share as finders. US Attorney Holabird, on instructions, asked that everything go back to Spain without salvage. His alternative request was that the Africans be returned to Africa if found to have been imported illegally. Judson ordered an inquiry into exactly where the schooner had been seized.
entries.source_note: FJC case history (19 Sept session, Holabird's alternative); Prologue (NARA) on Holabird's document; Prologue n. 17 (Ruiz and Montes libels of 18 Sept).

entries.headline: Murder charges dropped; habeas corpus refused
entries.digest: Baldwin and Staples sought a writ of habeas corpus to free the Africans, starting with the three girls. Justice Smith Thompson held that US courts had no jurisdiction over acts on a Spanish ship on the high seas, which ended the murder and piracy charges. But he refused to release anyone while property claims were pending in the district court. He reminded the defence that the Constitution protected property in slaves.
entries.source_note: FJC case history (17 Sept grand jury; 23 Sept adjournment); NPS timeline (23 Sept); Barber (18–23 Sept habeas proceedings).

entries.headline: Adams notes the case of the fifty-three
entries.digest: In his diary Adams took up the story of the African captives who had risen at sea and been brought into Connecticut by a US vessel. He was a congressman with a long record of fighting the gag rule on antislavery petitions, and he followed the case closely from then on. It was a year before anyone asked him to take part.
entries.source_note: MHS selected diary entries: 1 October 1839, diary 42 p. 221 (description as given by MHS).

entries.place: New Haven jail and the New York waterfront
entries.headline: Counting to ten along the docks
entries.digest: In the jail Gibbs held up one finger and a coin until Grabeau gave the Mende word, and so learned the numbers to ten. He walked the New Haven and New York wharves counting them aloud to every African sailor he met. On HMS Buzzard he found Covey and Charles Pratt, who understood. The Buzzard's captain let them go to New Haven, and by early October the captives had someone to speak for them.
entries.source_note: Famous Trials Gibbs biography; Barber (Covey found aboard the Buzzard in October 1839); NPS timeline gives 9 Sept for the finding. Day unrecorded.

entries.headline: The interpreter's deposition
entries.digest: James Covey gave a sworn deposition. He described his own origins in the Mende country, his kidnapping and his release by a British cruiser, and confirmed that he could speak with the captives in their own language. He was the first witness who could say from inside the language that these were Mende people only lately out of Africa.
entries.source_note: Yale News 2016 (Covey deposition dated 4 Oct 1839, Baldwin Family Papers); content as summarised in Connecticut History and NEHS articles.

entries.headline: Through Covey: the hold of the Tecora
entries.digest: Speaking through Covey, Grabeau told how they had been chained in pairs by the hands and feet in the slaver's hold and kept there day and night. He described being forced to eat, the beatings, and many dying on the way to Havana. The others standing round confirmed it. A reporter took it down in summary English for the Journal of Commerce.
entries.quote: kept in that situation day and night
entries.source_note: Barber (1840): Grabeau's narrative given 7 Oct 1839; Journal of Commerce narrative translated by Covey (Famous Trials newspaper accounts). Words passed through Covey and a reporter.

entries.place: New Haven (letter to the Journal of Commerce)
entries.headline: George Day writes up the captives' stories
entries.digest: George E. Day, a young Yale-trained teacher working with the captives, sent the Journal of Commerce a letter dated New Haven, 8 October. It summarised what the men had told him through Covey: their villages, how each was seized, and the voyage. Barber reprinted it the next year. Day and Yale students had begun daily lessons in English and scripture.
entries.source_note: Barber (1840): Mr. Day's letter to the Journal of Commerce dated New Haven, 8 Oct 1839.

entries.headline: The claimants are arrested
entries.digest: On Tappan's initiative, suits for assault and false imprisonment were brought in New York in the names of Cinqué and Fuliwa, and Ruiz and Montes were arrested at their lodgings. Two days later Tappan wrote to the English Quaker Joseph Sturge that they would test the question in American courts. Montes was soon released and left for Cuba. Ruiz stayed in jail rather than post bail, which made him a martyr in the Southern press.
entries.source_note: NPS timeline (17 Oct arrests; 22 Oct hearings); Linder (letter to Sturge 19 Oct 1839); FJC case history (Ruiz jailed until Feb 1840).

entries.headline: Plea: born free, kidnapped, seized in New York waters
entries.digest: The Africans came into court as parties for the first time. Baldwin and Staples pleaded that they were free persons kidnapped in Africa and unlawfully held in Cuba. They argued that Gedney had seized them in New York, a free state, so Connecticut had no claim on them. The British commissioner Richard Madden, back from Havana, swore on 20 November that newly landed Africans were routinely given false papers. Covey was ill, and Judson adjourned the trial to January in New Haven.
entries.source_note: FJC case history (19–21 Nov session); Linder (Madden deposition 20 Nov 1839); Famous Trials trial page (testimony 20 Nov, adjourned to 7 Jan 1840).

entries.headline: A ship made ready for Cuba
entries.digest: Secretary of State Forsyth arranged with the Navy for a vessel to be ready at New Haven to carry the Africans to Cuba as soon as the district court ruled. The administration expected Judson to decide for Spain. Sending them away at once would have made any appeal useless.
entries.source_note: NPS timeline (2 Jan 1840); FJC case history (Navy ship prepared for quick delivery).

entries.headline: The President signs the order to the marshal
entries.digest: Van Buren signed and Forsyth countersigned an order to the Connecticut marshal, Norris Willcox. It told him to deliver the 'negroes late of the Spanish schooner Amistad' to Lieutenant John S. Paine of the Navy and help put them aboard the schooner Grampus. The order was to be the marshal's authority. It never had to be carried out.
entries.source_note: Order dated 7 Jan 1840, Gilder Lehrman Collection GLC05636.01 (AM Digital catalogue description); Linder (order of 7 Jan).

entries.headline: The trial opens before a packed room
entries.digest: Judson opened the trial in New Haven before a very large crowd. The district attorney announced that Spain's claims were now joined with those of the United States. The defence filed its answer to all the libels that day, signed by Staples, Baldwin and Sedgwick as proctors for the Africans. Witnesses began testifying that the captives were plainly Africans, not Cuban-born slaves.
entries.source_note: NPS timeline (7 Jan); FJC case history; proctors' answer dated 7 Jan 1840 (National Archives at Boston; Teaching With Documents).

entries.headline: In the witness box: 'not taken in battle'
entries.digest: With Covey beside him, Sengbe told the court he came from Mendi and had been seized by countrymen while working on a road. He had not been taken in war and had not sold himself, and he had a wife and three children. He described Lomboko, the chains from Africa to Havana and aboard the schooner, hunger, and a sailor's beatings. He told of offering Gedney's men the ship if they would take them to Sierra Leone. The courtroom listened to the man the papers had been describing for months.
entries.source_note: NPS timeline (Cinqué testifies 8 Jan); NY Journal of Commerce, 10 Jan 1840 (NJSBF handout). Words through Covey and a reporter.

entries.headline: Grabeau and Fuliwa confirm the story
entries.digest: Grabeau and Fuliwa testified after Sengbe, again through Covey, to their kidnapping, the passage to Cuba, the sale and the revolt. Their accounts matched in the points the defence needed: recent arrival from Africa, the Lomboko factory, the Tecora and a short stay in Havana.
entries.source_note: NPS timeline (Grabeau and Fuliwa also testify); Famous Trials trial page (joint testimony heading). Exact day of each not confirmed.

entries.headline: Names that had never been to Cuba
entries.digest: Gibbs testified that the captives' names were ordinary Mende words for places and things. Men who had lived for years in Cuba, he said, would have had their names worn into Spanish forms. Judson cut him short, saying he was fully convinced the men were from Africa and that it was idle to deny it.
entries.source_note: Famous Trials Gibbs biography (testimony and Judson's interruption, as reported). Day not confirmed.

entries.headline: The Grampus drops anchor
entries.digest: The navy schooner Grampus arrived in New Haven harbour while the trial was still under way. Tappan and his allies took it as proof that the executive meant to remove the Africans before any appeal.
entries.source_note: Linder, 'Stamped with Glory' (Grampus arrives 9 Jan 1840).

entries.headline: Born free: the district court's decision
entries.digest: Judson ruled that the court had jurisdiction because the schooner was taken on the high seas. He found that the Africans were born free, had been kidnapped, and were never lawfully slaves under Spanish law, so their passports were false. He awarded Gedney salvage of one-third on the ship and cargo but not on the people, and rejected the Long Island claim. Antonio, the captain's slave, was to be returned to Spanish authority. The Africans were to be delivered to the President for return to Africa under the 1819 Act.
entries.quote: natives of Africa, and were born free
entries.source_note: NPS timeline and FJC case history (decision 13 Jan 1840); decree text as given by Famous Trials. The decree recorded on 23 Jan carries the quoted words.

entries.headline: The decree is entered, and the government appeals
entries.digest: The formal decree was recorded, ordering the Africans delivered to the President for transport to Africa. On instructions from Washington, the district attorney at once appealed every part except Antonio's return. The Grampus sailed without them.
entries.source_note: Prologue (NARA) n. 29 (Final Records, 23 Jan 1840); FJC case history (government appeal).

entries.headline: 'Executive usurpation': the Grampus becomes a scandal
entries.digest: The Hartford Courant accused Van Buren of trying to override the court and send the Africans to Cuba to be sold. It cited the Grampus waiting off New Haven as proof. Other letters in the Connecticut press spoke of foul play and of a threat to the independence of the federal courts. The case was now a campaign issue in an election year.
entries.source_note: Hartford Courant, 10 Feb 1840, as given in Famous Trials newspaper accounts; New London Gazette letter (undated) on 'foul play'.

entries.headline: A formal affirmance, so the Supreme Court can decide
entries.digest: Baldwin moved to dismiss the government's appeal, arguing that the United States had no interest of its own in Spanish property claims. Justice Thompson denied the motion and affirmed the district court's decree pro forma, without deciding the merits. This sent the case quickly to the Supreme Court. The captives stayed in custody and in the autumn were moved to a new jail at Westville.
entries.source_note: FJC case history (29 Apr 1840; motion to dismiss; pro forma decree); Barber and NPS give the same date. FJC places the court at Hartford, Barber at New Haven.

entries.headline: 'A case of life and death': Adams says yes
entries.digest: Ellis Gray Loring of Boston and Lewis Tappan called and asked Adams to join Baldwin before the Supreme Court. He pleaded his age, his work in the House and thirty years away from the bar, and offered advice instead. They pressed him. He agreed to argue if his health held, and Tappan left him two scrapbooks of clippings on the case.
entries.quote: it being a case of life and death, that I yielded
entries.source_note: JQA Digital Diary, 27 Oct 1840, diary 41 p. 113 (MHS); quote as given by MHS Beehive post.

entries.place: New Haven and the Westville jail
entries.headline: Adams visits his clients in jail
entries.digest: On his way to Washington, Adams stopped at New Haven, talked over strategy with Baldwin and went out to see the captives. His diary records the visit and the meeting. He had promised Baldwin by letter a week earlier to do what he could for 'these unfortunate men'.
entries.source_note: MHS selected diary entries: 17 Nov 1840, diary 41 p. 160 (visit to prisoners and meeting with Baldwin); Adams to Baldwin, 11 Nov 1840 (Gilder Lehrman/Quartex). Details of whom he met not checked against the page.

entries.headline: Preparing, and hunting the altered translation
entries.digest: Adams recorded his work on the case among his House business. Two days earlier he had charged in the House that a published translation of a Cuban document had been doctored to make the captives look like long-time slaves. A committee was appointed to look into it. He was preparing to make the executive's conduct, not just Spain's claim, part of his case.
entries.source_note: MHS selected diary entries: 12 Dec 1840, diary 41 p. 185; NPS timeline (10 Dec 1840 charge and committee).

entries.headline: Kale writes to Mr. Adams
entries.digest: Writing for all the captives, Kale told Adams they were born in Mendi and had spent only about ten days in Havana, against what Ruiz claimed. He asked Adams to put to the court what they had done wrong to be kept in prison. He described their reading of the Gospels and daily writing. He said some Americans called the Mendi people crazy or dull because they could not talk English. They did not want to go to Havana or be killed. They wanted freedom, teachers and a way home. Kinna wrote to Adams the same month.
entries.source_note: Kale to JQA, 4 Jan 1841, Adams Family Papers (MHS); transcription printed in Papers of the New Haven Colony Historical Society 4 (1888), pp. 354–55 (TeachIt CT PDF); MHS Object of the Month Jan 2003.

entries.date_display: February 1841 (one letter dated 9 Feb; another dated '29 Feb')
entries.headline: Letters against the jailer
entries.digest: In letters signed with his name, Cinqué complained of the jailer, Stanton Pendleton. He accused him of threatening the Mendi people, calling all Black people worthless, and spreading stories that they stole and drank rum. He asked Tappan to tell Mr. Adams and to pray that they might be freed and go home to their friends. One letter is dated 9 February. The other bears the impossible date '29 February 1841'. These were written in English with help.
entries.source_note: Yale News 2016 (letter of 9 Feb 1841, Baldwin Family Papers); NJSBF handout from Tulane Digital Library (letter to Tappan dated 29 Feb 1841).

entries.place: Supreme Court chamber, US Capitol, Washington
entries.headline: Gilpin for the treaty; Baldwin for Spanish law
entries.digest: Attorney General Henry Gilpin opened for the government. He argued that the ship's papers, signed by Spanish officials, must be taken at face value or international commerce would collapse. Baldwin answered over two days that under Spain's own laws Africans brought in after 1820 were free. He argued that the United States could not act as agent for foreign slave-owners. He finished on 23 February.
entries.source_note: NPS timeline (22 Feb opening; Baldwin concludes 23 Feb); FJC case history (Gilpin's argument).

entries.headline: Four and a half hours, and dissatisfaction
entries.digest: Adams began by appealing to the Court as a court of justice and then attacked the executive's 'sympathy' for the Spaniards. He described the order to the marshal that would have sent the captives away. He invoked the copy of the Declaration of Independence hanging in the courtroom. He spoke for about four and a half hours. That night his diary admitted he had not lived up to what the public expected of him.
entries.quote: I did not I could not answer public expectation
entries.source_note: JQA diary 24 Feb 1841, diary 41 p. 259 (quote as given by MHS Beehive post); printed Argument (S. W. Benedict, 1841), Avalon Project.

entries.headline: A justice dies; the Court adjourns
entries.digest: Justice Philip Pendleton Barbour of Virginia died suddenly during the night. The Court suspended the argument, and Adams's speech was cut in half for nearly a week. The Amistad was decided by the seven remaining justices.
entries.source_note: FJC case history (arguments suspended after Barbour's death on 25 Feb; resumed 1 Mar).

entries.headline: Adams concludes with the absent judges
entries.digest: Adams spoke for about four more hours to finish his argument. He closed by recalling the justices and counsel he had seen in that court when he first argued there decades earlier, all now gone. He hoped the present judges would be judged well in their turn. Gilpin replied the next day.
entries.source_note: MHS selected diary entries: 1 Mar 1841, diary 41 p. 264; MHS Beehive (about four hours on 1 Mar); FJC (closing arguments 2 Mar); printed Argument (1841). Content of the closing passage from the printed Argument, not checked against the page this session.

entries.headline: 'These negroes ought to be deemed free'
entries.digest: Story read the Court's opinion. The Africans had been kidnapped and unlawfully carried to Cuba, he held, so they were never Spanish property. The ship's papers were a fraud, and the 1795 treaty could not take away their equal rights. Because they had arrived in possession of the ship and not as imported slaves, the order to deliver them to the President was reversed, and they were simply to be released. Justice Henry Baldwin dissented without opinion.
entries.quote: these negroes ought to be deemed free
entries.source_note: United States v. The Amistad, 40 U.S. (15 Pet.) 518 (1841); NARA DocsTeach; FJC case history (holdings; dissent); Office of the Historian (treaty 'never could have been intended to take away the equal rights').

entries.headline: The verdict in the diary, and a note to Tappan
entries.digest: Adams recorded the Court's decision freeing the Africans. The same day he sent Tappan the news in a short, jubilant letter. Tappan's committee published it two days later.
entries.source_note: MHS selected diary entries: 9 Mar 1841, diary 41 p. 272; Linder (Adams writes Tappan 9 Mar; committee announcement 11 Mar). Wording of the letter varies between printings.

entries.headline: To his wife: a speech of power and sarcasm
entries.digest: In a letter home Story told his wife the case had been decided for the Africans. He called Adams's argument extraordinary for its power and its bitter sarcasm, but said it had ranged far beyond the record and the questions before the Court. Admiration and judicial disapproval sit together in the letter.
entries.source_note: Story to Sarah Wetmore Story, printed in W. W. Story, Life and Letters of Joseph Story (1851), vol. 2; wording as widely cited (e.g. Wheelan, Mr. Adams's Last Crusade). Exact date of the letter not seen.

entries.headline: Asking for a ship home, and being refused
entries.digest: Adams tried to get the government to carry the freed Africans home in a public vessel, as the 1819 Act had allowed for rescued captives. The new Tyler administration declined. Their passage would have to be paid for privately.
entries.source_note: MHS selected diary entries: 18 Mar 1841, diary 41 p. 281 (attempt to secure passage). Outcome from Linder and NPS (privately funded voyage).

entries.headline: Free, and taken in at Farmington
entries.digest: The news reached the captives at Westville and they were released by order of the circuit court. They moved to Farmington, where abolitionist townspeople housed them, and they worked and studied for about eight months. Through the summer they toured with Tappan's committee to raise money for the voyage. Foone (Fonne), one of the men, drowned that summer in a pond at Farmington.
entries.source_note: FJC case history (release; Farmington); Linder (eight months at Farmington; Fonne drowned summer 1841); famous-trials chronology (March–November 1841 at Farmington).

entries.headline: 'Yet my conscience presses me on'
entries.digest: Twenty days after the verdict, Adams reflected on his age and failing powers and on how much remained to be done against slavery and the slave trade. He wrote that he could not stop. The Amistad was a beginning for him, not an end.
entries.quote: Yet my conscience presses me on
entries.source_note: JQA diary 29 Mar 1841, diary 41 p. 292 (quote as given by MHS Beehive post).

entries.headline: A Bible from Cinqué
entries.digest: Adams received a Bible sent by Cinqué and others of the Mende as a farewell gift and thanks. It is still at the Adams National Historical Park in Quincy.
entries.source_note: NPS detailed timeline (19 Nov 1841; Bible at Adams NHP).

entries.headline: Farewell on board the Gentleman
entries.digest: Thirty-five survivors left Farmington by packet boat and boarded the barque Gentleman at New York with missionaries, including the Reverend William Raymond and the Reverend James Steele, for a 'Mendi Mission'. Covey sailed with them. Tappan went aboard to say goodbye and recorded a final prayer and leave-taking.
entries.source_note: NPS timeline (departure 27 Nov 1841, missionaries named); Linder (farewell on board in quarantine off Staten Island dated 4 Dec 1841). The two dates are not reconciled here.

entries.headline: Landfall at Freetown
entries.digest: The Gentleman reached Sierra Leone after about seven weeks at sea. Sengbe and the others found the country disrupted by war and slaving, and many soon left the mission. Lomboko, the slave factory where they had been sold, was destroyed by a British raid in 1849.
entries.source_note: NPS timeline (January 1842); famous-trials chronology (mission problems; Lomboko raided Dec 1849). Exact landing day not confirmed.

claims.claim: The Africans 'rose and murdered' the captain and crew and were trying to sail back to Africa.
claims.evidence: New London Gazette, 26 Aug 1839 (Famous Trials newspaper accounts)

claims.claim: Libel for salvage on the Amistad, its cargo (about $40,000) and the Africans as slaves ($25,000).
Murder and piracy referred to the grand jury; warrants of seizure and arrest issued.
Cinqué said to have told his comrades it was better to die than be a slave (source unstated).
claims.evidence: New York Sun advertisement and lithograph (LOC 2003690782)

claims.claim: Spain demands the ship and Africans under the 1795 treaty and their trial in Cuba.
claims.evidence: Spanish minister's note to Forsyth (NPS timeline; Office of the Historian)

claims.claim: Ruiz and Montes libel the Africans as their property.
Circuit court: no jurisdiction over the alleged crimes at sea; habeas corpus denied.
Through Covey: captives chained day and night on the Tecora from Africa to Havana.
Plea that the Africans were born free, kidnapped, and seized in New York, not Connecticut.
President orders the marshal to hand the Africans to Lt. Paine for the Grampus.
claims.evidence: Order of 7 Jan 1840, Gilder Lehrman GLC05636.01

claims.claim: Through Covey: seized on a road in Mendi, 'not taken in battle', never sold himself.
claims.evidence: NY Journal of Commerce, 10 Jan 1840 (report of testimony)

claims.claim: Africans born free and kidnapped; to be delivered to the President for return to Africa.
claims.evidence: Decree recorded 23 Jan 1840, RG 21; FJC; NPS

claims.claim: The Grampus shows 'Executive usurpation' over the federal court.
Born in Mendi, ten days in Havana; asks what wrong they have done to be held.
claims.evidence: Kale to JQA, Adams Family Papers (MHS); printed 1888

claims.claim: The executive's 'sympathy' for the Spaniards and its order to the marshal betray justice.
claims.evidence: Argument of John Quincy Adams (New York: S. W. Benedict, 1841)

claims.claim: Africans kidnapped, not property; ought to be deemed free and released, not sent to the President.
claims.evidence: United States v. The Amistad, 40 U.S. (15 Pet.) 518

convergences.label: The seizure off Culloden Point
convergences.note: The Navy's account is of a rescue and a prize. The Gazette's is of mutiny, murder and a fearsome leader. Cinqué, who tried to escape by jumping into the sea, offered the ship in exchange for passage to Sierra Leone, but no one aboard could understand him.

convergences.label: The court on the Washington's deck
convergences.note: Three kinds of claim met in one place: a judge charging murder, an officer counting salvage and two buyers expecting their property back. The Africans had no lawyer and no interpreter, and no one heard their side.

convergences.label: Spain's demand and Tappan's first visit
convergences.note: On the same day Spain's minister asked Washington to send the 'cargo' to Cuba and Tappan stood in the New Haven jail describing Cinqué's 'noble air' for the New York press. The diplomatic and the public campaigns began together.

convergences.label: An interpreter arrives
convergences.note: Within four days Covey swore his deposition, Grabeau gave the first full narrative of the Middle Passage, and George Day sent the captives' stories to the Journal of Commerce. After five weeks of silence the record suddenly holds the Africans' own accounts, though in a reporter's English.

convergences.label: The President's order and the opening of the trial
convergences.note: In Washington, Van Buren signed the order to put the Africans aboard the Grampus. In New Haven, Judson opened the trial that was supposed to make it lawful. Two days later the Grampus arrived and the abolitionists drew their own conclusions.

convergences.label: The captives testify
convergences.note: Sengbe, Grabeau and Fuliwa told the story of their seizure through Covey, and Gibbs testified that their names were unchanged Mende words. The linguist's evidence and the witnesses' own accounts supported each other, and the judge stopped hearing more.

convergences.label: A letter to counsel
convergences.note: Kale's letter in his own English reached the old statesman who was preparing to speak for him. Adams had told his diary he dreaded the task. Kale asked him to put one plain question to the Court: what wrong had they done?

convergences.label: Arguments before the Supreme Court
convergences.note: Baldwin argued Spanish law and Adams argued natural rights and the executive's misconduct. Story's opinion rested on Baldwin's Spanish-law ground and did not take up Adams's attack on the executive. Privately Story admired Adams's power but criticised how far he went beyond the record.

convergences.label: The decision
convergences.note: The opinion, the diary entry and the jubilant letter to New York were all written on one day. The Court freed the Africans on the narrow ground of Spanish law and treaty, and said nothing of Adams's charges against the executive.

ties.note: Gibbs found Covey on HMS Buzzard in New York by counting in Mende, and brought him to New Haven with the captain's leave.
Every word Sengbe spoke in court passed through Covey, a fellow Mende who had himself been freed from a slave ship.
Tappan and Loring called on Adams on 27 October 1840 and persuaded him to take the case. Adams wrote to Tappan the day it was won.
Kale wrote to Adams on 4 January 1841. Adams had visited the Westville jail seven weeks earlier.
Co-counsel. Adams wrote to Baldwin on 11 November 1840 and met him in New Haven on 17 November to plan the argument.
The men who claimed Sengbe as property had been his prisoners for eight weeks at sea. He in turn sued them for false imprisonment in New York.
Ruiz and Montes publicly thanked Gedney for their rescue, but his salvage claim was a charge on their 'property', and they appealed his award.
The administration prepared the Grampus expecting Judson to rule for Spain. He ruled against it, and it appealed his decree.
They were old acquaintances. Story ruled in Adams's favour on Baldwin's legal ground while privately criticising Adams's sarcasm.
Tappan had Ruiz and Montes arrested in New York on 17 October 1839, turning the claimants into defendants.
The Sun sold his portrait with a speech he probably never made, while the Journal of Commerce printed his testimony through Covey.
Grabeau gave Gibbs the Mende word for 'one', which started the search that found Covey.

threads_out.note: The Amistad Committee's Mende mission became the core of the American Missionary Association (1846). During and after the Civil War the AMA founded schools for freed people across the South, among them Hampton, Fisk and Atlanta.

Roger Sherman Baldwin was a grandson of Roger Sherman of Connecticut, who signed the Constitution at the 1787 Convention. The Amistad defence turned on the federal courts and treaty powers that Convention created.
John Quincy Adams, whose diary records the Amistad argument, was US minister in St Petersburg in 1812 and kept the same diary through Napoleon's invasion of Russia.

The Congress of Vienna's declaration against the slave trade (February 1815) led to Britain's 1817 treaty with Spain banning the trade to Spanish colonies from 1820. Baldwin and Story relied on that treaty to show the captives could not be lawfully held in Cuba.

images.title: Joseph Cinquez, the brave Congolese Chief, who prefers death to slavery
images.caption: Lithograph sold by the New York Sun within days of the seizure and advertised on 31 August 1839, with a speech attributed to Cinqué whose source is unknown. It shows how the press created a hero before anyone could speak with him. 'Congolese' was a guess. He was Mende.
images.credit: Moses Yale Beach, lithographer (probably drawn by James or Isaac Sheffield); Library of Congress Prints and Photographs

images.title: Joseph Cinqué, Leader of the Amistad Captives
images.caption: Nathaniel Jocelyn's oil portrait, painted in New Haven while Cinqué was in custody. The artist was the brother of Simeon Jocelyn of the Amistad Committee. The National Archives exhibit shows a reproduction of the original in the New Haven Museum.
images.credit: Nathaniel Jocelyn; New Haven Colony Historical Society (New Haven Museum)

images.title: Cinqué, Chief of the Amistad Captives
images.caption: John Sartain's mezzotint after Jocelyn's portrait, commissioned along with the painting by the Black Philadelphia abolitionist Robert Purvis. The bamboo staff and draped cloak present Cinqué as a classical republican hero.
images.credit: John Sartain after Nathaniel Jocelyn; Bowdoin College Museum of Art (2021.15)

images.title: Kale's letter to John Quincy Adams
images.caption: The manuscript letter written by Kale at Westville on 4 January 1841, the captives' fullest statement in their own English, sent seven weeks before Adams argued their case.
images.credit: Adams Family Papers, Massachusetts Historical Society

images.title: A History of the Amistad Captives (Barber, 1840)
images.caption: Barber's New Haven pamphlet, with profile portraits of the captives traced by pantograph from wax figures modelled from life, a map of the Mende country and a diagram of the slave deck. It is a sympathetic contemporary compilation, not a neutral record.
images.credit: John Warner Barber; Documenting the American South (UNC), from the Duke University copy
